newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's first post-apartheid census draws to end.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's first post-apartheid census draws to end.

text.p: South Africa formally ended its first post-apartheid census on Thursday but officials complained they had been hampered by guard dogs and anti-crime razor wire.
"Our monitoring shows that more than 90 percent of the country has been enumerated," Pali Lehohla of the state Central Statistical Service (CSS) said.
He said the count would be extended for a week in some areas, particularly the commercial heartland province of Gauteng, where the three-week process had faced delays.

Lehohla's colleague Theresa Pretorius said security systems, including alarms and dogs, had prevented access to many households in Gauteng where violent crime has fuelled a siege mentality among many residents.
The census, which began on October 10 with the counting of the homeless at state-sponsored midnight street parties, involved 80,000 enumerators and cost 356 million rand ($75.4 million).
It was the first attempt to tally accurately everyone in the country -- particularly blacks whose numbers were estimated from aerial photographs in previous apartheid-era head counts.
Pretorius said the first comprehensive results were expected by the end of January. A full assessment of the population should be complete by the end of next year.
It is hoped the census will help President Nelson Mandela's government address apartheid-era backlogs in housing, schools and health care.
